chapter: Blues origins and the club and radio scene
title: Origins of blues and jazz, postwar singers, Dewdrop, promoters and radio
summary: One long block: blues from the black church and slavery, Jelly Roll Morton's claim, Buddy Johnson, Arthur Prysock, Louis Jordan, Big Joe Turner at the Dewdrop, promoter August Jackson, new radio stations and Club Desire.

bands.name: Andy Kirk and His Clouds of Joy

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: Because this was what you would call spiritual rejuvenation. A lot of people didn't understand what was happening with the blues, especially some of the white bands who just started picking up on the blues into the late 80s, that the blues really came out of the black church. And, well, prior to that, the sacrifices that blacks made were harmed from the soul because they paid so many dues. And then, as I talked with my old great uncles from way back when they spoke with their ancestors and relatives during the days of slavery, when you had as many women as you wanted. But sometimes some of the slaves fell in love with some of the slave women. And when the slave master sold them off, then this is where the blues officially was born. The blues, as we know it today, the feeling, the emotional drive between the woman and the man because they had gotten together for the emotional feeling of dedication toward each other. But when they were separated, that's when the blues fell in. And so this is some of the things that happened as far as the structure of blues. And from blues, then what happens? Then you had something that when they got back together again, you had what was known as a jazzy feeling, an up-tempo kind of thing. Now, we got a guy from New Orleans who claimed that he invented jazz. Well, you know who I'm talking about. We're talking about Lou. Jelly Roll Morton. Jelly Roll Morton. Jelly Roll. Jelly Roll. But I can't totally go along with that. I think he had a lot to do with it because he was probably one of the first guys to write music and put it on paper. And from there, the embellishment and the extended technical craftsmanship of jazz music was then handed down to Louis Armstrong, Kid Ory, and Sidney Desveen and all the rest of the guys at that time. Now, we had a new development that was happening in the 40s right after the war. We had bands coming down to New Orleans like in 45 and 46. Buddy Johnson came down here, and he brought a new kind of singer. He brought, I'm trying to think of the gentleman's name right now. I'm trying to not waste a lot of time. Arthur Prysock was his name, who was a balladeer. Now, Arthur could sing deep, sensuous blues, and also he had some similar tonal qualities like Billy Eckstein. And sometimes the people who would probably go to shows, they would try to balance between the two. But they were different singers altogether. But yet, they had a certain type of twilight delivery into the structure of their music and the songs that they would sing. But they had certain parallels together. And along comes, well, of course, there was Louis Jordan, who probably could do almost anything with music. But he had that happy medium, Chattanooga choo-choo and all of this kind of stuff, red beans and ham hocks. And just whatever Louis would do, he would let it all hang out. I can remember doing a show back in the 1970s with Louis Jordan before he passed. Wallace Davenport, myself and a few others, we were at the Marriott Hotel. And I think it was the last time that Louis Jordan came to New Orleans. But prior to that, he had done movies. The movies were shown at the Palace and also at the Lincoln Theaters right here in the city of New Orleans. And, of course, you could not say that the 20th century had its evolutionary force of any kind of blues and jazz without Big Joe Turner. Big Joe Turner was a premier technician of his day when it came to singing variety kinds of blues with emotional feeling also. And he spent quite a bit of time here in the city of New Orleans. Most of the time when he first came here, he stayed at the Dewdrop. Well, that was Frank Pannier's facility. You had the Patterson Hotel. You had the Rogers Hotel. You had the Page Hotel. You had the Northside Hotel. But he stayed at the Dewdrop Hotel because that's where he was playing with Frank Pannier. When Frank was the modern-day technician of the South who promoted for the first time, I think, big-name groups coming into New Orleans. Now, prior to that, now, you've got to remember, we go back to say that Kev Calloway played at the Elks. We could say that Andy Quirk played at the Gypsy Tea Room and at the Coliseum. These are the venues which were open at that time, but they didn't do it on a continuing basis. Then along, I think we had a chance, you and me, we never got a chance to talk about August W. Jackson, who was the first black to be licensed to promote shows. Now, August Jackson, before Rip Roberts and these guys got together, he promoted the real licensed shows. He brought in Count Basie. He brought in Mahalia Jackson. Well, Mahalia had sung here before, but she was a big name at the time. And then August started bringing in Brother Joe May. Then here in 1950, then Jackson was hitting his stride between 1948 and to the 50s because you had the birth of WMRY radio station, which is now WYLD. And then in December of 1950, you had WBOK. So you had two venues of exposure from radio electronics to deliver across vast areas, happenings of things in New Orleans. Jazz, blues, entertainment, the Dewdrop was in its glory. Then you had all these big names coming in. So many things were happening. Of course, the premier club, no doubt about it, was the godfather of all clubs, was the Dewdrop. Of course, the most beautiful club, in my estimation, to be built in its day, I think, was Charlie Armstead's Club Desire. That's when the Zire Street Court was running down the street there. But a couple of years later, they cut it out. Something started happening between business politics and so forth and so on. New Orleans started changing.
